catalog_locator: Kapitonov 2019, ch. 2 Phonology, sec. 2.6 'Stress', pp. 32-35 (quotes from pp. 33, 34, 35). Coleman 1982, sec. 1.10 'Word-level stress', thesis pp. 21-24.
catalog_quote: Stress in Kunbarlang is not contrastive, i.e. it does not serve the differentiating function. It is signalled primarily by higher pitch of the stressed syllable vowel and also by greater intensity (in dB). [...] The stressed antepenult in figure 2.1 notwithstanding, the most robust pattern is for the primary stress to fall on the penultimate syllable, if the word is longer than one syllable. In monosyllables the stress will fall on the only syllable. [...] However, frequently there are exceptions. Let us focus on verbs, which can get very long and also offer complex morphological structures. [...] Other examples of the primary stress falling on non-penultimate syllables are the antepenultimate on the stem (2.20a), final (also on the stem; 2.20b), or both [...] This variation does not seem to betray any systematically organised metrical structure. At the present stage of research, I find that Kunbarlang primary stress is fixed lexical, with a tendency towards penultimate. This means that all morphemes are inherently specified for stress location (no-stress specification being one possibility), with some limited variation possible in discourse [...]. Furthermore, from the current data it appears plausible that stems take precedence over affixes, so that the primary stress falls on the stem, and affixes receive secondary stress. Stems must be allowed the no-stress specification, in which case an affix receives the primary stress, as in (2.19).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and by default falls on the penultimate syllable (sole syllable of monosyllables), cued by pitch and intensity; but placement is not fully predictable, especially in prefixed verbs, so the author treats stress location as lexically specified per morpheme with a strong penultimate tendency, stems normally taking primary stress and affixes secondary. Coleman 1982 (p.21, same dir) independently states plain penultimate primary stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Kapitonov p.35: secondary stress 'tends to go leftwards on alternating syllables from wherever the primary stress is placed', with larger gaps in long words; no word with more than three audible stresses; occasional clash. Coleman 1982 p.21: secondary stress on the third preceding syllable (fifth from the end of the word), weaker pitch rise and lengthening.
new_statements.exceptions: Kapitonov pp.34-35: primary stress may sit on the pronominal prefix rather than a mono- or disyllabic stem (ngadda-rdam, ka-kidanj), on the antepenult of the stem (nga-bak-rdukkume), or word-finally (ngadda-djarrang); variant barramimbanj ~ barramimbanj 'woman'; antepenult stress not driven by syllable weight; sec. 2.7.1 =bonj / -ma shift stress from gender prefix onto root -buk. Coleman pp.22-24: intramorphemic sonorant elision pulls stress back one syllable; reduplication stresses the first syllable of each copy (gobeng-gobeng irregular initial stress); first syllable of each polysyllabic argument prefix stressed in long verbs; pretonic syllables 'run together' in 7+ syllable words. Author stresses that no instrumental study has been done.
new_statements.domain_note: Grammatical/morphological word incl. pronominal prefixes and enclitics (e.g. na-wuk=bonj stressed on penult of the clitic group); tokens drawn from both isolation and connected speech, author reports little contextual variation. Coleman frames word stress as demarcative (marks word boundaries).
new_statements.identity_note: Both primary sources describe Kunbarlang (kunb1251) as a whole. Kapitonov 2019 is based on fieldwork mainly at Warruwi (Goulburn Island) and Maningrida, 2015-2018; Coleman 1982 lists six named Gunbalang dialects (djimbilirri, gurrigurri, gumunggurdu, marrabanggu, marranumbu, gunguluwala) but gives one stress description for the language. Harris 1969 data from Oenpelli, Maningrida and Goulburn Island. No sub-glottocode distinction needed.

tone.quote: Stress in Kunbarlang is not contrastive, i.e. it does not serve the differentiating function. It is signalled primarily by higher pitch of the stressed syllable vowel and also by greater intensity (in dB). Vowel length does not seem to pattern together with these metrics, and where there is a mismatch, I find identification of primary stress placement rather challenging. Figure 2.1 below shows the spikes of both pitch (specks) and intensity (contour line) on the stressed antepenultimate syllable in the verbal word nganjrdukkume ‘I’ll cut it’, realised as [ãɲˈɖukːume].
tone.summary: No tone analysis; pitch enters only as the main cue of non-contrastive, mostly penultimate word stress (one pitch/intensity track shown) and in sentence intonation. The 23 forms are stress-marked.
tone.says: No tone analysis; pitch enters only as the main cue of non-contrastive, mostly penultimate word stress (one pitch/intensity track shown) and in sentence intonation. The 23 forms are stress-marked.

tone.quote: Primary stress occurs on the initial syllable of each root except when compounds are formed of more than one root, then primary stress occurs on the penultimate syllable. [...] The basic intonation pattern is a gradual rise culminating in a swift fall at utterance final position for statements, and a gradual rise to utterance final for most questions. There is a great variety of tempo patterns and intonation patterns which were not analysed because of the limited scope of this paper.
